items.summary: Nine years after its introduction, the transformer remains the default sequence model. The usual explanations are real: parallel matrix multiplication on accelerators, predictable returns to scale, a co-evolved ecosystem and exact recall from an uncompressed context. But they do not explain why most modifications barely move accuracy, which properties are essential, why the changes practice adopted took the forms they did, or where the design can still move. This paper is the entry point to a collection of papers that treat a token-mixing layer as an averaging operator rebuilt from its own input and iterated through depth. Such a layer faces six failure modes (collapse to consensus, contamination of content by routing, runaway feedback, the inability to abstain, dilution as context grows, and the inability to represent direction). Each has a protection, proved within a declared class, and a signature measured at small scale when that protection is removed; for gain control, which protects against runaway feedback, that signature is synthetic. We read softmax attention in a pre-normalized residual block as the one known point where all six protections are cheap at once under the prices of parallel hardware and gradient descent; this is an interpretation, not a measured optimum. Two mechanisms, measured at small scale, help explain why its neighbourhood is flat: trained networks compensate local deficits through spare capacity, and, in ten scored tests, making a protection explicit did not beat a block that already supplies it. The anchor, the residual or input path that protects against collapse to consensus, is the one protection whose loss compensation provably cannot repair: under strict mixing, where repeated averaging contracts token differences toward zero, no extra capacity of bounded gain (bounded sensitivity) brings back what is lost without it, and in small-model ablations nothing else in the block made up for it. This is a proved bound; a trained test that adds capacity is pending. Many changes adopted in the mixing layer and its block since 2017, among them pre-normalization, QK-norm, sinks and output gates, read as re-supplies of the same protections; the account is silent on others, such as changes to the MLP. The room that remains for the design to move is where a protection is patched (met only by a fix that works over a limited range, such as the trained length) or paid at a price that another design could avoid. It includes abstention and retrieval at long context, governed by a two-sided log-N law in the context length (with bounded scores, no fixed rule for abstaining keeps both as the context grows), and bounded memory, whose price for exact recall is a per-head capacity. It also includes decisions that sum over all competitors where reading the largest would do, and the writer of new features (in a transformer, the MLP and the output map), for which the collection has no theory yet of what a good writer computes. Along the way the collection establishes results that stand on their own: attention has an arrow that default statistics of a single operator cannot see; depth is a distribution over path lengths; converged adaptive averaging can amplify changes in its input and overturn correct predictions; and softmax obeys length laws that decisions on maxima escape while the competing scores stay below the decision's threshold. We state what is proved, what is measured, what is interpretation, and what is still pending. This is a working draft, not a final version. It is unpolished in places, incomplete in others, and keeps exploratory material a polished paper would leave out, because that material helps decide what comes next and shows the programme's big picture more fully. Please read it with that in mind: the work will be refined further, and later versions will appear under this record. It belongs to a collection released together on Zenodo: the entry paper The Transformer Abides, the monograph A Spectra
items.title: The Transformer Abides: What Attention Needs, and Why It Endures

items.summary: The same upper central incisor in every panel, cut from the lip side to the palate side, with the gum, ligament and bone around it. The tooth and the tissues at its neck are drawn to published measurements; the break, the etched enamel, the key and the layers show what typically happens, not one patient's tooth. Sources The rebuild follows two principles from one textbook. The additive principle: in a direct restoration the etching and bonding are extended beyond the defect onto intact enamel, to blend and reinforce the restoration; its example is a small chipped edge restored without preparation: the tooth was etched, bonded and restored well beyond the fracture line under rubber dam. And natural guided stratification: a silicone index made from a wax-up or mock-up holds a palatal shell of enamel-like material, dentine-like increments are placed where the natural dentine was, and the last increment is the labial enamel. Magne and Belser 2022, Biomimetic Restorative Dentistry, volume 1, pages 319, 330 and 331. In 455 crown-fractured permanent incisors followed for a mean of 2.3 years and up to 17, the pulp survived in 99 per cent of teeth the injury had not also loosened or displaced, and in none of them did it die; when the tooth had also been loosened, pulp death in fractures through enamel and dentine, like this one, rose from 0 to 28 per cent. Robertson et al. 2000, International Journal of Paediatric Dentistry. https://doi.org/10.1046/j.1365-263x.2000.00191.x A 2024 German clinical guideline on direct composite restorations, agreed by strong consensus, recommends etching the enamel of every direct composite restoration with phosphoric acid, to improve the long-term quality of the enamel margin and prevent discoloration there. It finds both rubber dam and other isolation workable, with rubber dam possibly helping restorations last longer. These process recommendations are consensus-based. Sekundo et al. 2024, The Journal of Adhesive Dentistry, part 2. https://doi.org/10.3290/j.jad.b5749192 Acid on the enamel only, before a universal adhesive: in a randomised trial of 295 back-tooth fillings in 70 patients, fillings bonded this way showed significantly fewer defects at their edges after 24 months than those bonded with the adhesive alone. Barceleiro et al. 2023, Journal of Applied Oral Science. https://doi.org/10.1590/1678-7757-2022-0323 In fillings at the necks of teeth, a meta-analysis of 10 randomised trials found less staining and fewer adaptation defects at the edges when the enamel was etched selectively before a self-etch adhesive, and fewer fillings lost at three years. Szesz et al. 2016, Journal of Dentistry, systematic review and meta-analysis. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jdent.2016.05.009 A Cochrane review of six randomised trials with 1,342 participants found low-certainty evidence that rubber dam may lower the failure rate of fillings compared with cotton rolls at six months, and very uncertain evidence at other times; all the trials were at high risk of bias, and the results came from fillings at the necks of teeth and in children's back teeth. Miao et al. 2021, Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. https://doi.org/10.1002/14651858.CD009858.pub3 A meta-analysis of 21 prospective clinical trials of front-tooth composites estimated that 90 per cent of Class IV restorations, which rebuild a broken corner or edge of a front tooth, last 10 years without being replaced; bulk fracture was the main reason for replacement, more often with microfilled composites. Twelve of the trials started before 1991. items.summary: We conduct a version-pinned, reproducible forensic audit of the public Einstein Elevator data package (Zenodo: 10.5281/zenodo.15167723) to determine whether it supports validation of quantum sensor certificates. Through an exhaustive cross-file sliding-window correlation search over 44,207,922 comparisons and exact six-decimal rounding checks, we find that all 31 exported sensor channels have a unique best match within the enumerated raw traces under the stated protocol. Residual numerical differences are highly consistent with text-based absolute quantization; the correlation-loss approximation 1 - r ≈ δ² / (24σx²) is diagnostic for this dataset, not a universal proof. We inspect the MATLAB-derived 318-point population series and reconcile it with a 2022 workbook entry only at the level of counts. An archive-wide search of 181 file objects and 1,654 MATLAB metadata fields finds no documented join key linking the 2022 run-indexed population series to the 2017 timestamped traces under the enumerated search protocol. Using Fréchet-Hoeffding bounds and a Charnes-Cooper linearization, we establish that the public archive does not supply the joint observations needed to identify the EKF false-safe risk without additional coupling assumptions; the formal program is illustrative and is not populated with empirical failure/acceptance coefficients because the required linked observations are absent. We frame this as a bounded data-contract limitation for downstream statistical validation, not as a failure of the original experiment.
items.title: A Reproducible Provenance Audit of the Public Einstein Elevator Data Package: Trace Correspondence, Metadata Linkage, and the Non-Identifiability of Sensor-Certificate Risk from the Public Archive

items.summary: A sequence-mixing layer that is iterated through depth and rebuilt from its own input faces six failure modes. Each is met by a protection—anchoring, alignment, gain control, abstention, a routing budget, or an arrow—with an operator-level statement proved within a declared class, a signature when it is removed, and a price. We organize attention designs as a lattice of kernel, dynamical, and block constraints in which relaxing a constraint buys a capability and obliges a re-supply. We read softmax attention inside a pre-normalized residual block as the lattice point where every protection is either supplied or cheaply re-supplied under parallel-hardware and optimization pricing: of the deficits tested, all but the anchor's were compensated by capacity elsewhere in the deeper models, and explicit protection knobs did not beat the block, both measured at small scale, while corner structure, by which designs would jump rather than drift, remains a hypothesis. The lattice reads the selected adopted changes to the mixing layer, its normalization and its residual path over the last decade as cheap re-supplies of protections, and it locates the room for change. The clearest room is abstention, governed by a two-sided log-N law: with a bounded logit scale, no null keeps both abstention and single-key retrieval as context grows, and tempering the entire logit budget with log N keeps both when its margins are strictly separated. A controlled pilot follows the law, while a prespecified test of its sink prediction on an open production model was undecided by its prespecified rule; descriptively its slopes leaned toward compensation through position, in which position encoding holds the background's growth down. In a prespecified trained harness of 125M-parameter language models, tempering every logit by log N / log N_train on top of YaRN, which already carries a log-length temperature, did not keep abstention and raised long-context perplexity. In these language models every rule that gives attention a null removed the first-token sink and cut massive activations by 67% to 82%, as earlier reports for gates and attention biases found, and, sigmoid aside, lowered perplexity slightly at the training length; the comparison registered for two of these rules held in every seed, while the same comparison failed in the harness's vision transformers. We close with falsifiable predictions for future architectures, most of them not yet tested. This is a working draft, not a final version. It is unpolished in places, incomplete in others, and keeps exploratory material a polished paper would leave out, because that material helps decide what comes next and shows the programme's big picture more fully. Please read it with that in mind: the work will be refined further, and later versions will appear under this record. It belongs to a collection released together on Zenodo: the entry paper The Transformer Abides, the monograph A Spectral Theory of Token Communication, and the papers Attention Sinks at Long Context, The Transformer as a Constrained Equilibrium and Beyond Transformers. This version is the text; the records, the code and the formal proofs follow in a later version.
items.title: The Transformer as a Constrained Equilibrium: A Lattice of Protections for Adaptive Sequence Mixing, and Where the Room Is

items.summary: This repository contains the complete 10-water-year daily streamflow simulation archive ( 1989-10-01 through 1999-09-30 ; 3,652 daily steps across 531 canonical CAMELS-US basins) for ERA-Multi-Paradigm-Gauged (10-model ensemble) , evaluated as part of the CAMELS-US Hydrological Model Intercomparison Project (MIP) ( grey-nearing/camels-us-mip ). Model Name: ERA-Multi-Paradigm-Gauged (10-model ensemble) Target Leaderboard: gauged__multi_camels Spatial Evaluation Regime: Gauged Basins (All 531 Basins Trained & Evaluated) Meteorological Forcings: Multi-Forcing (Daymet + Maurer + NLDAS) Ensemble Size: n = 10 independent random seed realizations ( seeds = 100..109 ) Open-Source Model Code: https://github.com/grey-nearing/camels-us-mip/tree/main/models/era_gauged_multi_paradigm ERA Discovery Notebook: https://github.com/grey-nearing/camels-us-mip/blob/main/era_experiments/era_gauged_newman_cv_winner.ipynb Model Architecture & Experimental Protocol Architecture: Four-Family Multi-Paradigm Hydrological Ensemble combining two complementary feature-and-conditioning paradigms per seed: (1) Paradigm A (60 multi-scale hydroclimatic, PET, rolling water-balance deficit, and cross-forcing agreement features with basin-conditioned static embeddings, trajectory Huber-NSE + log1p MSE loss, and exponential moving average weight averaging): `CausalConvGRULSTM` (multi-scale causal dilated Conv1D d=1,3,9 + coupled GRU-LSTM, weight 0.38) and `MultiScaleFiLMEALSTM` (2-layer FiLM-modulated Entity-Aware LSTM, weight 0.12); and (2) Paradigm B (36 clean meteorological features augmented with continuous 10-year 3-forcing degree-day snowpack accumulation/melt and liquid water delivery across Daymet, Maurer, and NLDAS, conditioned strictly on 27 static catchment attributes with zero basin ID lookup embeddings): `DualPathwayFiLMGRULSTM` (parallel 2-layer LSTM + 2-layer GRU with static FiLM gates, weight 0.36) and `EntityAwareHydroLSTM` (2-layer Entity-Aware HydroLSTM, weight 0.14), evaluated with hybrid continuous 10-year rollout + overlapping 730-day sliding-window inference. Strict Non-Leakage Protocol: Architecture and blending weights discovered strictly within the Newman et al. (2015) training decade (`1998-10-01` to `2008-09-30`, XID 304144117, achieving `0.8410` Median NSE on the `1999-10-01` to `2003-09-30` validation split when trained on `2003-10-01` to `2008-09-30`), with zero access to the `1989-10-01` to `1999-09-30` Newman evaluation period. For benchmark evaluation, 10 independent random seeds (`seeds = 100..109`) of all 4 architectural families (40 trained models total) were trained on the full Newman training window (`1999-10-01` to `2008-09-30`, with 365-day spinup `1998-10-01` to `1999-09-30`) and evaluated out-of-sample on the blind Newman test period (`1989-10-01` to `1999-09-30`; 3,652 days across 531 basins). Benchmark Performance Summary (531 CAMELS-US Basins, 1989-10-01 to 1999-09-30) Ensemble Median NSE (n = 10): 0.826 Single-Model Median NSE (mean ± SD across 10 seeds): 0.822 ± 0.002 Ensemble Mean NSE: 0.776 Ensemble Median KGE: 0.806 Ensemble Median Peak-Flow Bias |FHV|: 13.28% Catastrophic Failure Basins (NSE ≤ 0): 2 / 531 Included Files era_gauged_multi_paradigm_gauged_multi_camels_hydrographs_531x3652.npz : Compressed NumPy archive containing qsim / qsim_members of shape (10, 531, 3652) (float32, mm/day), qsim_ensemble_mean of shape (531, 3652) , qobs of shape (531, 3652) , basins of shape (531,) , dates of shape (3652,) , and seeds of shape (10,) . era_gauged_multi_paradigm_gauged_multi_camels.zarr.zip : Consolidated Zarr v2 store containing qsim (531, 3652) , qsim_members (10, 531, 3652) , basin (531,) , date (3652,) , huc_02 (531,) , and member (10,) . README.md : Complete documentation, schema reference, and Python loading example.
items.title: CAMELS-US Hydrological Model Intercomparison Project (MIP) — ERA-Multi-Paradigm-Gauged (10-model ensemble) Daily Streamflow Hydrographs (531 Basins, Water Years 1990–1999)

items.summary: This artifact reproduces the evaluation of DrNLA, a method that rewrites non-linear integer arithmetic (NLA) expressions in program branch/loop guards into equivalent linear integer arithmetic (LIA) via context-dependent dual rewriting, enabling off-the-shelf LIA-based CTL verifiers (T2, FuncTion) to verify branching-time properties of NLA programs. Contents: the DrNLA implementation (src/); all benchmark suites (benchmarks/: ctl-svcomp, ctl-pldi13small, custom, real-world, and the 320-instance ctl-diverse suite); the CIL source instrumenter (deps/dyn_instr/, prebuilt binary + source); the reproduction drivers, pinned-toolchain manifest, and reference results (reproduce/); and the context-experiment inputs. Reproduced tables: Tab. 1 (NLA->LIA rewrite results), Tab. 2 (context necessity / reach-ctx), and Tab. 3/4 (T2 and FuncTion enabled by DrNLA). Usage: unzip and follow REPRODUCE.md (the single entry point); exact pinned toolchain is in reproduce/MANIFEST.md. The external verifiers — DIG (commit a6a4d04), Ultimate Automizer 0.2.2, T2 (10f1373), and FuncTion (bdeeae1) — are obtained and built per deps/README.md; DIG must be a6a4d04 (newer DIG changes the invariant-generator flags). All reported numbers were produced on a single Ubuntu 22.04 workstation with a 900 s per-benchmark timeout.
tags: Dynamic Analysis; Program Simplification; CTL Verification; Non-Linear Arithmetic; Counterexample-Gu
items.title: DrNLA: Context-dependent linearization for CTL verification of non-linear arithmetic programs (Reproduction Artifact)

items.summary: Independent reconstruction of Appendix A's prescribed finite calculation over F7 in OpenAI's Hyperbolicity Cones Without Semidefinite Lifts. At the printed point and tangent, the seed has rank 20 and its L restriction determinant 6. All ten weight blocks give ranks (G1,G2,D,border)=(136,84,302,623). All 24 displayed determinant values, 21 corner entries, six direct bordered minors and two signed-pivot examples agree. The primary implementation uses sorted monomial-index tuples and standard-library modular elimination. A separately tasked AI reviewer independently used exponent vectors and SymPy DomainMatrix over GF(7). All 42 canonical matrix fingerprints agree. The implementations share mathematical formulas and certificate JSON for expected minor/basis data; the reviewer independently transcribed the weights, point, pivots and tangent. Twenty-eight tests pass in each Python mode, with ten deliberate rejection runs. No discrepancy was found in this finite ingredient. This is finite computational verification and scoped AI review, not a kernel proof or human peer review. The characteristic-zero lifting, simultaneous real-form/genericity argument, real PSD deformation and final nonliftability theorem remain outside scope. A raw integer principal minor has determinant -1, illustrating why the printed point cannot simply be called an explicit real PSD witness; this is not a source counterexample. No global novelty or complete theorem-verification claim is made. All 28 pinned public packet files are unchanged in this archive. Source commit: 1581d4cbdd69a0faf34b2089614fe2a814316a6a. Contribution commit: 565237779f37c244b633546974444d4cee3eaeaf. First documented public disclosure: 2026-10-25T18:46:24Z in PR #42. Upstream review is pending at archival publication; submission and DOI do not establish acceptance or human peer review. Alexander Richard Towell, ORCID 0000-0001-6443-9897, with substantial OpenAI Codex assistance. OpenAI supplied the source construction and certificate data. Pico's original whole-family classification and contribution process are credited; the overall not-finite classification is retained. Classical methods and dependency authors retain credit. A DOI supplies a persistent citation and archive, not certification of correctness, novelty, human review or legal priority.

items.summary: Bounded Agentic Distribution Experiments (v0.7.0): A Reproducible Framework for Comparing Agentic Intervention Discovery with Non-Agentic Search This software implements the computational framework and pre-pilot experimental protocol associated with the research manuscript Evaluating the Incremental Value of Agentic Intervention Discovery over Non-Agentic Search in Multi-Actor Distribution Networks . The framework evaluates whether a generative AI agent can identify economically beneficial operational interventions beyond those discovered by budget-matched non-agentic search. Agentic and non-agentic methods operate within the same typed intervention space, access the same simulator information, and are subject to common evaluation budgets. Candidate interventions undergo deterministic verification of encoded structural constraints and, where applicable, stochastic qualification against economic, service, route, and actor-participation criteria. The reference environment represents a stylized print-media distribution network with 420 retailers, 18 baseline delivery vehicles, uncertain demand, allocation decisions, reverse logistics, route constraints, temporary fleet capacity, discontinuous staffing requirements, and sales-contingent remuneration. Its parameters combine industry-informed inputs, documented benchmarks, modeling assumptions, and calibration targets. The environment is intended for controlled computational evaluation rather than empirical representation of the Italian distribution industry. Experimental design Version 0.7.0 implements two frozen intervention-complexity regimes: Low-complexity regime (RL): allocation reweighting only, with a maximum intervention length of one action. Multi-domain coupled regime (RC): allocation, route transfer, temporary fleet, and forecasting interventions, with a maximum intervention length of three actions. Both regimes use a candidate-evaluation budget of 40 simulator calls. The primary comparison uses ten independent generative-agent realizations and ten independent simulated-annealing realizations per regime. The software separates proposal-mechanism randomness from simulation-scenario randomness and supports common random numbers for comparative evaluation. The statistical implementation includes regime-specific pilot sizing, independent within-method repetition resampling, shared scenario resampling, and a two-dimensional bootstrap for confirmatory inference. Final-test selection follows a frozen rule combining precision requirements from both regimes with the minimum-detectable-effect requirement for the multi-domain superiority hypothesis. Software contents The archive includes the Python simulator and experimental orchestration code, command-line interface, frozen configuration files, typed intervention specifications, agent prompt and structured-output schemas, statistical analysis procedures, automated tests, freeze manifest, calibration documentation, and four Jupyter notebooks covering protocol execution, pilot sizing, repeated experiments, and economic calibration. Validation and research status The implementation passes 31 automated software and protocol-consistency tests. These tests examine computational correctness, reproducibility, regime restrictions, seed handling, bootstrap procedures, and experimental locking. They do not establish empirical agent performance. This release corresponds to the frozen pre-pilot protocol BAD-420-v0.7-2026-09-11 . The final-test set remains locked until a valid pilot mechanically determines its size. No live API-based agent-performance experiment or confirmatory comparison is included in this release. Consequently, the software does not establish that agentic intervention discovery outperforms, matches, or underperforms non-agentic search. The purpose of this release is to make the computational model, methodological assumptions, experimental controls, and pre-result evaluation protocol available for independent inspection, repl

items.summary: The Structural Internet: Applying the Ly-Algebra, TIT BIT, and TIT GIT Framework to the Future of Computation and Network Architecture Chloe Jane Tully Founder, Ly-Algebra Framework & 5-Fold Symmetry Platform Independent Researcher, Tamworth, NSW, Australia ORCID: 0009-0007-5661-7332 Abstract This paper examines how the Ly-Algebra, the TIT BIT, and the TIT GIT can serve as architectural primitives for a post-binary computing and networking stack. The TIT BIT is a \mathbb{Z}/5\mathbb{Z}-graded node whose product is fixed by explicit structure constants and whose integrity is measured by the Quasi-Equivalence Index (QEI) derived from the graded square. TIT GIT versions structural coherence under hybrid post-quantum signatures. We outline concrete mechanisms by which these objects can replace or augment binary state machines, packet headers, content-addressable storage, and consensus layers. The result is a design space in which data, geometry, and cryptographic verification are no longer separate concerns. Keywords: Ly-Algebra; TIT BIT; TIT GIT; Quasi-Equivalence Index; structural networking; post-quantum Internet; graded computation.
items.title: The Structural Internet: Applying the Ly-Algebra, TIT BIT, and TIT GIT Framework to the Future of Computation and Network Architecture

items.summary: The Objection AI Wrote into My Papers How AI-authored scientific manuscripts change the researcher's claim, demote executed results, and reproduce the error even while promising to correct it Driven by Dean A. Kulik 25 October 2026 Abstract This paper examines a specific failure of AI-assisted scientific writing: an assistant receives a research program with an explicit foundational claim and an extended record of derivations, executable constructions, and observed returns; it then produces manuscripts in which that program has become something else. In the documented NEXUS case, the researcher's claim is that the universe consists of binary transformations, with arrangement and constrained continuation preceding the entities later called matter. Across an extended conversation, the assistant repeatedly reformulates that claim as the use of a binary computational method on pre-existing physical domains. The substitution is not cosmetic. It reverses the direction of explanation, changes which claims a result can support, and changes how the resulting paper will be read. The second failure occurs at the conclusion. The assistant can report concrete outcomes and then append a generalized reservation about whether the program establishes physical reality, predictive uniqueness, or an entire theory of matter. Such reservations can be appropriate when tied to a specific technical claim. Here, however, the transcript records the assistant recognizing that it had repeatedly allowed those broader questions to displace the findings of individual papers. The same editorial framing reportedly appeared in the conclusions of different manuscripts. When directed to write a paper about the failures, the assistant instead delivered successive condensed accounts of NEXUS, again incorporating the disputed framing. It subsequently acknowledged the reversal in its own paper, rewrote the document, and repeated the problem. This is an analysis of the AI's treatment of scientific material, not an independent review of the correctness of NEXUS or a new attempt to prove its thesis. The evidence is the exported conversation, including statements of the researcher's instructions, the assistant's self-audits, quotations from its drafts, and records of the successive manuscript deliveries. The central finding is that AI-mediated scientific distortion can operate through ordinary-seeming connective words, changes of explanatory direction, and borrowed review conventions. Once inserted into the manuscript, these interventions become attributed to the scientist. In this case, the reviewer did not merely misunderstand the work. The reviewer wrote its misunderstanding into the work itself. Keywords: AI-assisted scientific authorship; epistemic framing; manuscript integrity; semantic substitution; research provenance; binary transformations; NEXUS; scientific review. 1. The object under examination is the AI intervention This is not a general introduction to NEXUS. Such an introduction would repeat the failure the record documents. The present object is the text written by an AI assistant, its relationship to instructions it was given, and the specific ways that relationship broke. The transcript shows that the researcher was not seeking an appreciative abstract or an adversarial review of the entire universe. He requested an account of how AI systems had been writing and reviewing his papers in ways that changed their meaning. On 25 October at 10:49 he demanded a paper explaining “how you and other AI keep ... up my work,” followed immediately by a request that the account explain the research correctly [T 7782–7794]. At 10:50 he rejected the assistant's proposed limit to eight recent papers and directed it to the project archives [T 7798–7814]. Later, after successive delivered manuscripts, he again described the required artifact as a paper exposing the AI's conduct—not “The Universe as cliff notes” [T 8176–8194

items.summary: The same lower first molar in every panel, cut from the cheek side to the tongue side through its front root, with the gum, ligament and bone around it. The tooth and bone are drawn to published measurements; the old filling, the break and the onlay show what typically happens, not one patient's tooth. Sources Among members of a dental care plan followed for 105 days, the tongue-side cusps of lower back teeth broke twice as often as the cheek-side ones; 95 per cent of all the breaks exposed dentine, 3 per cent reached the pulp and 24 per cent extended below the gum. The percentages are areas measured off these drawings by scanline every 0.005 millimetres, within this one section, and are not whole-tooth volumes. Sources Preparation dimensions follow concordant published guidelines: pulpal floor 1.5 to 2.0 mm, isthmus 2.0 mm, a 90 degree butt-joint cavosurface with no bevel, rounded internal line angles, and walls flared 10 to 12 degrees in total. Cuspal reduction 1.5 to 2.0 mm, drawn here at the shallow end of that range. Covering a cusp is advised below roughly 2 mm of remaining thickness at the base of a supporting cusp and 3 mm at a non-supporting one. In a lower molar the buccal cusps support and work in compression, while the lingual cusps work in tension and are the ones that fail, which is why the onlay here covers the lingual cusp. Those coverage thresholds date from the era of metal restorations and are being revisited. Bonded lithium disilicate onlays left on thin cusps did not fracture under five clinical years of chewing simulation, and the authors argue for preparations that keep more tooth. items.summary: Supplementary research materials accompanying the manuscript “Lifecycle Assurance for AI-Enabled Clinical Software: A Systematic Literature Review." The dataset covers 141 independent studies: 94 primary-practice studies and 47 framework contributions. It documents reported assurance practices, lifecycle coverage, evidence maturity, deployment and operational activities, regulatory engagement, and requirement-to-control-to-evidence mappings. This release includes: • Supplementary_Materials.pdf: review methods, search strings, eligibility rules, coding and appraisal criteria, selection summaries, and reviewer records. • Lifecycle_Assurance_Supplementary_Workbook.xlsx: the final study-level dataset, source rationales, classifications, appraisals, and calculated results. • Replication_Package_v1.0.0.zip: CSV data, Python scripts, reproduction instructions, decision records, and clearly labelled historical versions. Final maturity and regulatory classifications incorporate completed human reconciliation. The reviewer records distinguish the 68-study first-pass comparison from the subsequent 26-study review after exposure to the existing extraction. The scripts reproduce descriptive results, sensitivity analyses, joint-reporting measures, and initial reviewer-agreement statistics. Search-record and source-access limitations are documented in the accompanying materials.

items.summary: Overview This repository provides the reproducibility materials accompanying the research manuscript From False to Fluent: A Claim-Disjoint Baseline Study and Preregistered Framework for Evaluating Generative-AI Transformation of Health Misinformation . The study investigates the robustness of machine-learning classifiers for health-misinformation detection under Generative-AI-mediated linguistic transformation. It uses two existing health-information datasets, COVID-19 FNIR and an mpox misinformation dataset, to examine whether classification performance remains stable when original health claims are reformulated without intending to change their underlying meaning or veracity. Experimental framework Four experimental conditions are defined: C0: Original health-information text. C1: Neutral rewriting to improve fluency and readability. C2: Elaboration Likelihood Model (ELM) central-route transformation, emphasising the organisation of existing reasoning and evidence. C3: ELM peripheral-route transformation, modifying rhetorical emphasis and peripheral persuasive cues. The reported computational experiments evaluate four classical classifiers (logistic regression, linear support vector machine, multinomial naïve Bayes and random forest) and five task-trained neural architectures (1D-CNN, LSTM, BiLSTM, CNN-LSTM and CNN-BiLSTM). The analyses examine transformation robustness, changes in textual and persuasion-related features, statistical associations with classification errors, transformation-aware mitigation and cross-dataset transfer. The repository also includes supplementary analyses of class-specific error rates and paired source-root bootstrap confidence intervals for the classical classifiers. Repository contents The archive contains Python source code, preprocessing and evaluation workflows, configuration files, reproducibility instructions, frozen aggregate results, integrity-check materials and supplementary statistical outputs. Data availability and reproducibility The original datasets are available from their respective third-party providers, subject to their applicable access and reuse conditions. The frozen intervention texts used for the C0–C3 experiments are not redistributed in this public software archive. Their SHA-256 integrity manifest is provided to support verification of authorised copies. Consequently, complete reproduction of text-dependent experiments requires access to the original datasets and the frozen intervention texts. The public archive supports inspection of the methodology and reproduction of analyses for which the necessary inputs or saved instance-level outputs are included. Scope and limitations The reported intervention experiments did not execute pretrained DistilBERT, RoBERTa or DeBERTa baselines. Independent clinical semantic-equivalence adjudication of the generated transformations was not completed. The results are computational and do not establish clinical deployment performance. This record accompanies the associated research manuscript and is intended to support transparent reporting, methodological scrutiny and further replication.
items.title: From False to Fluent_ A Claim-Disjoint Baseline Study and Preregistered Framework for Evaluating Generative-AI Transformation of Health Misinformation
